text: Before you can understand what makes the quantum Fourier transform interesting, you need the ordinary, fully classical discrete Fourier transform cold — it's the same linear algebra, just acting on quantum amplitudes starting next lesson.

The DFT formula is X sub k equals the sum over j of x sub j times e to the 2 pi i j k over N — this course's positive-exponent convention, chosen specifically so it matches the quantum Fourier transform in Lesson 6 with no sign translation needed. Each output X sub k measures how much of frequency k is present, re-expressing the same information from the time domain into the frequency domain. Because the formula is linear, the whole transform is just one N by N matrix F applied to a vector, and the one-over-root-N factor out front makes F unitary — length-preserving, the exact form the quantum version will require.

Here's the exact matrix for N equals 4. Row k equals 0 is all 0.5's, since frequency 0 is the constant, or DC, component and every input contributes equally. Row k equals 2 alternates plus and minus 0.5 — the highest frequency a length-4 sequence can represent, flipping sign every single step. Rows 1 and 3 cycle through the four 4th roots of unity: 1, i, negative 1, negative i. This exact matrix reappears in Lesson 6 as the quantum Fourier transform for a 2-qubit register.

Nobody actually multiplies by this matrix directly at scale. Reading the formula literally costs O of N squared multiplications — for N equals one million that's a trillion operations, too slow for real use. The Fast Fourier Transform, discovered by Cooley and Tukey in 1965, restructures the same computation by recursively splitting even and odd indexed terms, exploiting the repeating structure of the roots of unity, and computes the exact same result in O of N log N — about 20 million operations instead of a trillion at that same size. This is entirely classical, no quantum computer involved, and it's one of the most important algorithms in all of computing.
Next lesson takes this identical matrix and applies it to quantum amplitudes instead of a classical list — the quantum Fourier transform's derivation.
